newsitem.title: ZAIRE: AMF signs minerals deal with Zaire rebels.
newsitem.headline: AMF signs minerals deal with Zaire rebels.

text.p: America Mineral Fields on Wednesday signed an agreement worth $1 billion with Zaire's rebels to buy the Kolwezi copper/cobalt tailings project and build a 200,000 tonnes a year zinc plant at Kipushi, the company's main shareholder said.
The agreement was signed by America Mineral Fields' Jean-Raymonde Boulle and by financial commissioner (finance minister) Mwana Nanga Mawampanga for the Laurent Kabila's rebel alliance.
Mawampanga said AMF had clearly won the tender for Kolwezi submitted to state-run mining company Gecamines, before the rebels took control of the country's mineral heartland.
AMF was one of several international mining companies, including Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd, Gencor Ltd and Iscor Ltd, who tendered to develop the project.
He said the projects had been awarded to AMF on the basis of the company's tender and nothing else.
"This government will respect international rules of conduct and will no longer tolerate corruption in the open tendering process," he said.

The Kolwezi project had the potential to produce around 6,000 tonnes of cobalt and 60,000 tonnes of copper a year over the next 20 years, said Mark Collins, AMF executive vice-president for exploration.
The company was looking for recovery rates of of 93 percent copper and 85 percent cobalt and was working on a cobalt price of just $6 per pound -- against the current price of around $24/lb.
Collins said the Kolwezi project could have a major impact on the international cobalt market and the company would be handling this very carefully.
World cobalt production is around 20,000 tonnes a year.
AMF said the Kipushi zinc smelter would also produce some 35,000 tonnes a year of copper and 400,000 tonnes of acid.
A second tailings project at Kipushi is at the study phase and AMF would also be exploring for copper/cobalt in this area.
In addition, the company had a $30 million contract to rehabilitate Gecamines' mines.
AMF principal shareholder Boulle said Zaire, with "fabulous yields," had the potential to be an African Chile and AMF's strategy was to get in on the ground floor.
"Our strategy as a group is to go for the highest grades and the largest deposits," he said.
Boulle said Kabila's rebels were now the de facto government in Zaire and he believed international recognition would follow the fact.
